screens.name: Settings
screens.purpose: The app's single screen: guides the user through granting the two required system permissions and lets them set the text-length bounds that gate the floating overlay button. Styling is fully automatic — there is no style list to manage; the screen shows a read-only gallery of the built-in mood looks.
key_ui_elements: Required System Permissions card with an Overlay row and an Accessibility Service row, each showing a granted/not-granted status icon and an 'Open' button that deep-links to the matching system Settings screen

App Language picker: a row of chips ('System Default' plus each supported language in its own native name) that overrides the app's UI language independent of the device's system language, applied immediately
Min/Max text length fields that gate when the floating overlay button appears

Automatic Styling card: a short explanation that the look is chosen from what the user types (mood, keywords, emoji), plus a horizontally-scrolling gallery of one live sample render per built-in mood (Funny, Sad, Romantic, Angry, Informative, Excited, Celebratory, Calm, Motivational, Grateful, Neutral). Nothing here is editable — there is no font, color, emoji, add, or remove control anymore.

features.name: Floating Style Overlay Trigger
features.description: A background AccessibilityService watches WhatsApp's actively focused editable field and shows one small floating overlay button whenever the typed text's trimmed length falls within the user-configured min/max bounds; the button auto-hides the instant the user leaves WhatsApp.
acceptance_criteria: Typing in a WhatsApp editable field shows a single overlay button once trimmed length is within [minTextLength, maxTextLength].
The overlay button never appears for an empty field, even if the user configures minTextLength down to 0.

The button is a perfect circle with a faint accent hairline border; while the user types it previews the auto-selected look, recolouring its fill and swapping its glyph to the detected mood's representative emoji, and falling back to a light near-white lavender fill with the ink-drop glyph (🫟) whenever the text matches no mood. Tapping it renders the current text with that automatically chosen style.
The overlay button hides immediately when length falls back out of bounds or focus moves to a non-editable view.

The overlay button hides immediately when the user leaves WhatsApp (home screen, another app, notification shade) and is not shown over any non-WhatsApp app; the soft keyboard opening over WhatsApp does not hide it, and returning to WhatsApp with the same field still focused restores it.
Dragging the button repositions it, and the position is remembered across hide/show cycles.
features.implementation_notes: TextMonitorAccessibilityService (AccessibilityService, @AndroidEntryPoint) listens for TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED/TYPE_VIEW_FOCUSED/TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED, tracks the current AccessibilityNodeInfo + text, and delegates the length check to a pure TextLengthEvaluator.isWithinBounds() so the boundary logic is unit-testable outside the framework. accessibility_service_config.xml carries no android:packageNames filter (so the service can observe the foreground app changing); styling is kept WhatsApp-only in code by ignoring every TYPE_VIEW_* event whose packageName != "com.whatsapp". handleForegroundWindowChanged() reacts to TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED: a non-WhatsApp, non-keyboard window (keyboard package resolved from Settings.Secure.DEFAULT_INPUT_METHOD, plus the app's own package) hides the overlay immediately, while a return to com.whatsapp calls activeNode.refresh() and re-shows the button only if that node is still an editable, focused field. isWithinBounds() requires trimmedLength > 0 in addition to the configured [minLength, maxLength] range (from the shared TriggerConfig), guaranteeing the overlay only shows once the user has actually entered text. OverlayWindowManager shows one FrameLayout button (a centered TextView glyph over a runtime GradientDrawable oval with a ~1dp accent-tinted hairline stroke; square view bounds + OVAL background keep it a perfect circle) via a single WindowManager TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY addView/removeView, with one drag-listener that repositions it and remembers the margins across hide/show. OverlayWindowManager.setAppearance(hex, emoji) / resetAppearance() recolour the oval's fill (GradientDrawable.setColor) and swap the TextView glyph live; the fill/glyph are remembered across hide/show so a rebuilt button keeps the last preview, and the default is a light lavender #F4F1FE fill with the ink-drop glyph 🫟. It no longer takes a styles provider or exposes refreshOverlay(). On every in-bounds text change, TextMonitorAccessibilityService.applyButtonPreview(text) calls AutoStyle.buttonHintFor(text) (non-random: detected intent's displayEmoji + its first look's backgroundColorHex, or null when no mood matches -> resetAppearance()) so the button previews the look a tap will produce. On tap, handleStyleButtonPressed() calls AutoStyle.styleFor(currentText) to derive the StyleConfig for the render.

features.name: Styled Image Rendering
features.description: Renders the captured text into a fixed 512x512 PNG square using the auto-selected StyleConfig — font, text color, solid or 2-stop gradient background, padding, and an emoji badge — with the font size auto-computed to fill the square and the text centered both horizontally and vertically. The square always has sharp corners (no border radius).
acceptance_criteria: The rendered bitmap is always exactly 512x512, regardless of text length.
Long strings wrap across multiple lines without overflowing the bitmap bounds, and font size shrinks automatically to fit.
Line wrapping only breaks at whitespace between words, never in the middle of a word, for any text whose individual words fit within the padded content width.
Text is centered both horizontally and vertically within the square.
An invalid hex color string falls back to a default color instead of crashing.
When a style's emoji field is non-blank, that emoji is drawn as a badge in the image's top-left corner, on top of the main text; a blank emoji field draws no badge.
The emoji glyph renders as a proper glyph (color emoji on modern devices) rather than a tofu box, regardless of which of the four bundled fonts the style uses.
features.implementation_notes: ImageRenderer.renderBitmap() delegates to buildFittedLayout(), which binary-searches the largest text size (12px-320px) whose StaticLayout both fits the padded content area's height AND keeps every whitespace-delimited word's measured width within the content width — a height-only check would accept sizes that only 'fit' by letting Android's line breaker split an overlong word mid-way, since the breaker forcibly wraps any word wider than the line rather than overflowing it. The chosen-size StaticLayout is then drawn centered onto a fixed 512x512 Canvas-backed Bitmap with a solid or LinearGradient square background (no rounded corners — config.cornerRadiusDp is no longer read). fontSizeSp has been removed entirely from StyleConfig, SettingsRepository, and the Settings UI, since font size is now always auto-computed. If config.emoji is non-blank, drawEmojiBadge() draws it last (on top of the main text) near the top-left corner using Typeface.DEFAULT rather than the style's own FontChoice — Android resolves emoji code points through the system-wide font fallback chain regardless of typeface family, so this reliably reaches the system's (vector/COLRv1 on modern devices) color emoji font instead of the four bundled type families needing their own emoji glyph coverage. generateStyledImageUri() writes the PNG to cacheDir/images and returns a FileProvider content URI. Rendering itself supports any Unicode script via Android's system font fallback (same mechanism the emoji badge uses) and lays out RTL scripts correctly via StaticLayout's default FIRSTSTRONG_LTR direction heuristic; the one known limitation is that the widest-word safety check splits on whitespace, so scripts without inter-word spaces (CJK, Thai, Lao, Khmer) can render at a smaller-than-optimal auto-fit size — see doc/i18n.md for the full analysis and the proper fix (Unicode line-break analysis instead of a whitespace split).

features.name: Clipboard Copy & Field Clear
features.description: Tapping the overlay button copies the rendered image to the system clipboard as an image/png ClipData and clears the original text field, so the user can immediately paste the styled image in place of what they typed.
acceptance_criteria: After tapping the overlay button, the system clipboard holds a ClipData whose item URI resolves to image/png, rendered with the style auto-selected from the text.
The originating text field is cleared via ACTION_SET_TEXT immediately after the copy.
A short confirmation Toast appears telling the user to paste.
features.implementation_notes: ClipboardManagerHelper.copyImageToClipboard() uses ClipData.newUri(contentResolver, label, uri) so the MIME type is resolved from FileProvider's own getType(). TextMonitorAccessibilityService.handleStyleButtonPressed() derives the StyleConfig via AutoStyle.styleFor(currentText), renders it, then calls AccessibilityNodeInfo.performAction(ACTION_SET_TEXT, empty string) on the tracked node.

features.name: Guided Permission Setup
features.description: The Settings screen live-checks both required permissions (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW via Settings.canDrawOverlays, the accessibility service via AccessibilityManager.getEnabledAccessibilityServiceList) on every onResume, and deep-links straight to the matching system Settings screen for whichever is missing.
acceptance_criteria: Returning to the app after granting a permission in system Settings updates that row to 'Granted' without needing to relaunch the app.
Tapping 'Open' on the overlay row launches ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION scoped to this app's package.
Tapping 'Open' on the accessibility row launches ACTION_ACCESSIBILITY_SETTINGS.
features.implementation_notes: PermissionUtils centralizes both live checks. MainActivity re-checks both in a DefaultLifecycleObserver.onResume() and triggers Play's In-App Review flow (InAppReviewHelper) the first time both permissions transition from not-fully-granted to fully-granted — a genuine positive completion point.

features.name: Content-Based Automatic Styling
features.description: The look of the rendered image is derived from the typed text instead of being user-configured. A fixed set of 11 moods (Intent enum: Funny, Sad, Romantic, Angry, Informative, Excited, Celebratory, Calm, Motivational, Grateful, and a Neutral fallback), each carrying 3–5 hand-tuned StyleConfig looks, is matched against the text's whole-word keywords, multi-word phrases, and emoji; the highest-scoring mood wins (Neutral when nothing matches) and one of its looks is picked at random per tap. The only user-configurable setting left is the min/max text-length trigger. The Settings screen shows a read-only gallery of one sample render per mood.
acceptance_criteria: Text containing a mood's keyword, phrase, or emoji renders in one of that mood's looks; text matching nothing renders in a Neutral look.
Phrases (e.g. 'thank you', 'you got this') outweigh a single competing keyword.
Keyword matching is whole-token and case-insensitive: 'misinformative' does not trigger the 'informative' keyword.
Repeated taps on the same text can produce different looks from the matched mood's set.
The Settings screen has no font, color, emoji, gradient, add-style, or remove-style control; it shows a scrollable read-only gallery of one sample render per mood.
The min/max text-length bounds still persist to DataStore across app restarts.
features.implementation_notes: AutoStyle.kt (data.model) holds it all with no Android dependencies so it is plain-JVM unit-testable: the Intent enum carries each mood's List<StyleConfig>; WORD_KEYWORDS / PHRASE_KEYWORDS / EMOJI_KEYWORDS map triggers to intents. Each intent's keyword list is grouped per language and covers all six languages the app's UI supports — English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Hindi — with accent-folded spellings alongside the accented forms; on-device translation was rejected because it would need an ML Kit model download in an otherwise offline no-network app. AutoStyle.detectIntent(text) NFC-normalizes and lowercases the text, tokenizes on runs of non-(letter|mark|number) so Devanagari tokens stay whole, scores every non-Neutral intent (phrase substring hit = 3, word-token hit = 1, emoji substring hit = 2), and returns the top scorer or Intent.NEUTRAL when all zero; ties break toward the earlier enum entry for stability. AutoStyle.styleFor(text, random = Random.Default) resolves the intent and returns intent.styles.random(random). AutoStyle.buttonHintFor(text) returns a non-random ButtonHint(emoji, backgroundColorHex) — the detected intent's displayEmoji plus its first look's backgroundColorHex — or null for Intent.NEUTRAL, so the floating overlay button can preview the detected mood as the user types without flickering. SettingsRepository now persists only triggerConfigFlow: Flow<TriggerConfig> under the `user_settings` DataStore (`min_length` / `max_length` keys); the `styles_json` key, stylesFlow, encode/decodeStyles, and DEFAULT_STYLES are gone. SettingsViewModel exposes only triggerState + updateTriggerConfig(). SettingsScreen's AutoStyleSection renders an explanatory Card plus a horizontally-scrolling Row of IntentPreview composables (one per Intent.entries), each calling ImageRenderer.renderBitmap() on Dispatchers.Default inside produceState. Covered by AutoStyleTest (12 JVM unit tests, including buttonHintFor's mood mapping, non-randomness, and null-on-no-match).

features.name: Multi-language UI Support
features.description: All UI chrome (permission copy, section titles, field labels, the Toast, font names) is externalized to string resources and translated into five languages beyond the English default (Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Hindi). An App Language picker on the Settings screen lets the user override the app's display language independent of the device's system language; the default 'System Default' option automatically follows whichever of the device's configured languages the app has a translation for, falling back to English otherwise — so language detection is Android's own resource-qualifier resolution, not custom logic.
acceptance_criteria: With no override selected, the app's UI language automatically matches the device's system language when a translation exists, and falls back to English otherwise, with no user action required.

Selecting a specific language in the App Language picker immediately re-renders the entire Settings screen in that language and persists the choice across app restarts, independent of the device's system language.
Selecting 'System Default' clears the override and reverts to automatic system-language matching.

All screen text — permission copy, section titles, field labels, button text, the copied-image confirmation Toast, and the four font names — is translated in every supported language; no hardcoded English string remains outside of the rendered sample preview text.
features.implementation_notes: res/values/strings.xml holds the English defaults; res/values-{es,fr,de,pt,hi}/strings.xml hold full translations, selected automatically by Android's locale-qualified resource resolution. FontChoice's label field became a @StringRes labelRes so font names localize too. LanguagePicker (SettingsScreen.kt) offers 'System Default' plus each supported language in its own native name; on API 33+ it reads/writes the override via Context.getSystemService(LocaleManager::class.java).applicationLocales directly (the same mechanism the OS's own per-app language settings use), with androidx.appcompat's AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales() as the pre-33 fallback — then calls Activity.recreate() itself since MainActivity is a plain ComponentActivity, not AppCompatActivity, so it doesn't get AppCompat's automatic recreation. AndroidManifest declares android:localeConfig="@xml/locales_config" (listing en/es/fr/de/pt/hi) so Android 13+'s own system-level per-app language settings page also lists this app, and a manifest-declared androidx.appcompat.app.AppLocalesMetadataHolderService with autoStoreLocales=true meta-data is required for AppCompatDelegate's static API to have a valid Application context to act on — omitting it makes setApplicationLocales() a silent no-op.

non_goals: No custom Input Method (IME) / system keyboard in this version — text is styled and cleared in place via AccessibilityService, not typed through a replacement keyboard.

No user-editable styles — no style list, no font/color/emoji/gradient pickers, no add/remove. The look is chosen automatically from the typed text; the built-in mood looks are fixed in code. paddingDp/cornerRadiusDp still exist on StyleConfig for the renderer but are fixed at their defaults.

No on-device translation of the typed text before keyword matching — the keyword tables carry the common triggers in the six supported languages directly, and emoji (language-independent) do most of the work.
No in-app purchases, ads, or any billing integration — the app is entirely free with no monetization.
No handwriting font creation — only the four bundled system type families (Sans Serif, Serif, Monospace, Cursive) are offered.
No cloud backend, accounts, or sync — all settings live in local DataStore on the one device.
No app-specific one-tap share target (e.g. WhatsApp) — the styled image is placed on the system clipboard for the user to paste anywhere themselves.

test_plan.scenario: Content-based intent detection and style selection
steps: Call AutoStyle.detectIntent with text carrying a mood keyword, a mood phrase, a mood emoji, a competing keyword+phrase mix, mixed case, non-English keywords (es/fr/de/pt/hi), an accent-folded spelling, an unmatched string, and a substring-of-a-keyword string.
Call AutoStyle.styleFor with a seeded Random for a matched text, repeatedly.
test_plan.expected: Keyword/phrase/emoji each select their intent in every supported language; accent-folded spellings still match; phrases outweigh a competing single keyword; matching is case-insensitive and whole-token ('misinformative' stays Neutral); unmatched and blank text return Intent.NEUTRAL. styleFor always returns a StyleConfig from the detected intent's own list and is deterministic for a fixed seed; buttonHintFor maps to the detected mood's emoji + colour, is non-random, and is null when nothing matches. (AutoStyleTest, 14 cases.)

steps: Call TextLengthEvaluator.isWithinBounds with lengths below, at, and above the configured min/max bounds.
Call it again with trimmedLength = 0 and minLength = 0.
test_plan.expected: Lengths strictly below minLength or strictly above maxLength return false; lengths equal to either bound or in between return true. A trimmedLength of 0 always returns false, even when minLength is 0.

test_plan.scenario: Rendered bitmap is always a fixed 512x512 square
steps: Render a short string and a long multi-sentence string with the same StyleConfig via ImageRenderer.renderBitmap on a connected device.
Compare the resulting bitmap dimensions.
test_plan.expected: Both the short and long string bitmaps are exactly 512x512, regardless of text length.

test_plan.scenario: Line wrapping never breaks a word mid-way
steps: Build the fitted StaticLayout (via ImageRenderer.buildFittedLayout) for a multi-word sentence long enough to wrap across several lines.
For each line break, check whether the character immediately before and after the break are both non-whitespace.
test_plan.expected: Every line break falls on whitespace between words; no line ends mid-word.

test_plan.scenario: Invalid hex colors fall back instead of crashing
steps: Render text with a StyleConfig whose textColorHex and backgroundColorHex are not valid hex strings.
test_plan.expected: Rendering completes and returns a non-empty bitmap instead of throwing.

test_plan.scenario: Emoji badge renders without breaking the fixed square
steps: Render the same text with a StyleConfig whose emoji is a non-blank string, and again with emoji blank.
test_plan.expected: Both renders succeed and return an exact 512x512 bitmap; the non-blank case has a visible glyph badge in the top-left corner, the blank case has none.

steps: Launch MainActivity via ActivityScenario so the process holds window focus.
From inside the resumed Activity, render an image and call ClipboardManagerHelper.copyImageToClipboard.
Read back ClipboardManager.primaryClip from the same focused Activity.
test_plan.expected: The primary clip's item URI matches the copied URI and its MIME type is image/png.

test_plan.scenario: App Language override applies immediately and persists
steps: Open Settings with the device's system language set to English and no override selected.
Tap a non-English language chip (e.g. Español) in the App Language picker.
Force-close and relaunch the app.
Tap 'System Default' to clear the override.
test_plan.expected: The whole Settings screen re-renders in the selected language immediately after tapping its chip; the override survives the relaunch; tapping 'System Default' reverts the UI to the device's system language (English).

steps: Grant both the overlay and accessibility permissions, confirm the overlay button appears while typing.
Revoke one permission from system Settings, return to the app.
test_plan.expected: The revoked permission's row reverts to 'not granted' on the very next onResume, and the overlay button stops appearing until it's re-granted.

test_plan.scenario: Automatic style matches the message mood
steps: In WhatsApp, type a clearly funny message (e.g. 'haha this is hilarious 😂'), tap the overlay button, and paste.
Repeat with a romantic message ('I love you so much ❤️'), an informative one ('FYI: meeting agenda for tomorrow'), and a gibberish string with no mood words.
Tap the button several times on the same funny message, pasting each result.
test_plan.expected: Each paste shows an image whose colors/emoji fit the message's mood — playful for the funny one, warm/pink for the romantic one, clean/neutral for the informative one, and a plain Neutral look for the gibberish. Repeated taps on the same message can produce different looks from that mood's set.

steps: Open Settings and scroll through the whole screen.
test_plan.expected: There is a permissions card, an App Language picker, min/max length fields, and an 'Automatic Styling' card with a scrollable read-only gallery of one sample render per mood. There is no font/color/emoji/gradient picker and no Add Style / Remove Style button anywhere.

fields.name: id
fields.notes: random UUID default; no longer meaningful (styles are not a persisted, id-addressed list anymore) but kept so the data class and the renderer/tests are untouched

fields.name: font
fields.notes: maps to an Android generic Typeface family name

fields.name: backgroundColorHex
fields.notes: solid color, or gradient start color

fields.name: paddingDp
fields.notes: default 32 — not exposed in the UI

fields.name: cornerRadiusDp
fields.notes: default 24 — unused by the renderer (square always has sharp corners); not exposed in the UI

fields.name: emoji
fields.notes: badge drawn in the image's top-left corner; blank means no badge

data_model.notes: No longer persisted. StyleConfig is now purely the render input produced by AutoStyle.styleFor(text): each Intent hard-codes 3–5 StyleConfig looks in code. DEFAULT_STYLES, the `styles_json` DataStore key, and SettingsRepository.encode/decodeStyles are removed.

fields.name: name
fields.notes: one of FUNNY, SAD, ROMANTIC, ANGRY, INFORMATIVE, EXCITED, CELEBRATORY, CALM, MOTIVATIONAL, GRATEFUL, NEUTRAL (NEUTRAL = fallback for unmatched text)

fields.name: displayEmoji
fields.notes: representative emoji for the mood, shown as the gallery label context

fields.name: styles
fields.notes: 3–5 hand-tuned looks; AutoStyle.styleFor picks one at random per tap

data_model.notes: Defined in data.model/AutoStyle.kt with no Android imports so it is plain-JVM unit-testable. Paired with static WORD_KEYWORDS / PHRASE_KEYWORDS / EMOJI_KEYWORDS maps (trigger -> Intent) used by AutoStyle.detectIntent() to score the typed text.
The only persisted user setting left (keys `min_length` / `max_length` under the `user_settings` Preferences DataStore).

libraries.purpose: Android Kotlin extensions and compatibility helpers
Per-app language override (AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales) for the App Language picker
Local key-value storage for the text-length TriggerConfig
Coroutines for DataStore flows and the accessibility service's settings collector
Dependency injection into the Application, Activity, and AccessibilityService
Play In-App Review prompt after first successful permission setup

positioning: Type anywhere — any app, any field — and turn what you typed into a beautifully styled image with one tap on a small floating button, ready to paste right back in.

design_system.typography: Google Fonts 'Fraunces' (serif, expressive) for in-app headings/branding, Material 3 default type scale (Roboto Flex) for all other UI chrome and body text — never used for the rendered style output itself, which uses the font of the auto-selected mood style.
design_system.theme_notes: Dark mode follows the system default: light theme uses background #F7F5FF / surface #FFFFFF / on-background #1C1B1F; dark theme uses background #16151F / surface #201F2C / on-background #E7E1FF.

store_listing.title: InkSend: Style Any Text
store_listing.icon_prompt: Create a 1024x1024 Android app icon for InkSend, a text-styling utility app. Rounded-square adaptive icon style, indigo background (#5B47E0), a simple white fountain-pen nib icon with a short flowing ink stroke. Flat vector design, high contrast, no text, no brand logos, no photorealistic elements.
store_listing.long_description:
InkSend turns anything you type, in any app, into a beautifully styled image — font, colors, gradient, and an emoji badge chosen to match your message — ready to paste back in with one tap.

Just start typing in a text field. Once your message is long enough, a small floating button appears. Tap it, and InkSend reads the mood of what you wrote — funny, sad, romantic, excited, grateful and more — picks a matching look, renders your exact words as a styled image, copies it to your clipboard, and clears the field. A long-press and Paste (or your keyboard's clipboard suggestion) drops the image right back in.

There's nothing to set up. No style list to build, no colors to pick — the styling is automatic, and font size always auto-fits your text. The one setting is which message lengths should trigger the button.

Everything happens on your device. No account, no ads, no subscription — InkSend is completely free.
store_listing.short_description: Type a message and paste it back as an image styled to match its mood — free, no ads, no account.

project_context: This spec describes an independent, alternative Android app you are building from scratch to compete with an existing incumbent app on Google Play — not a modification, clone, or reskin of the incumbent's own code, assets, or branding. Use the incumbent only as a market reference (via the report data below), and design working_name/package_id/store_listing/design_system so the result is clearly its own product.
build_instructions:
chmod +x ./gradlew
./gradlew clean
./gradlew testDebugUnitTest
./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore inksend-upload.jks -storetype JKS -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 -alias upload -dname "CN=InkSend Upload,O=AppyFYI,C=US" -storepass changeit -keypass changeit
RELEASE_STORE_FILE="$PWD/inksend-upload.jks" RELEASE_STORE_PASSWORD="changeit" RELEASE_KEY_ALIAS="upload" RELEASE_KEY_PASSWORD="changeit" ./gradlew bundleRelease
